Imagine you say, "Torturing innocent children for fun is wrong." Now ask yourself: is that statement wrong because you personally dislike it, or is it wrong whether or not you — or anyone — likes it or believes it?

Moral objectivism is the philosophical position that says: moral facts are real and exist independently of what any person, culture, or society thinks or feels about them. Moral truths aren't just opinions. They aren't just cultural preferences. They are objective — meaning they hold true even if every single person on Earth were to disagree.

Think of it like mathematics. The statement "2 + 2 = 4" is true regardless of whether you believe it, feel it, or were raised to accept it. Moral objectivism says morality works the same way. "Gratuitous cruelty is wrong" is true in the same mind-independent sense as a mathematical truth — it doesn't need your approval to be true.
The Word "Objective" — What It Really Means Here

The word objective is the key, so it's worth pinning down precisely.

Something is objective if its truth doesn't depend on the observer — on any one mind, group of minds, culture, or feeling. The mass of the Moon is objective: it's what it is regardless of whether anyone measures it or believes in it.

Something is subjective if its truth does depend on the observer. "Chocolate ice cream is delicious" is subjective — it's only true relative to the person making the claim.

Moral objectivism says that moral claims — statements about right and wrong, good and evil — fall into the objective category, not the subjective one.
What Moral Objectivism Is Claiming, Exactly

Moral objectivism makes at least one or more of these related claims:

1. Some moral statements are genuinely true or false. "Slavery is wrong" isn't just a preference, like saying "I prefer jazz to classical." It is a claim with a truth value — and it's true, full stop.

2. Moral truths don't depend on what individuals believe. If a person or even an entire society believes that slavery is acceptable, they are mistaken. The fact that they believe it doesn't make it true, just as believing the Earth is flat doesn't make the Earth flat.

3. Moral truths don't depend on what cultures think. A society that practiced human sacrifice in ancient times was not doing something "right for them." They were doing something objectively wrong, even if they didn't know it.

4. Moral truths exist independently of human existence altogether. Even in a world with no humans to observe them, "unnecessary suffering is bad" would still be true — just as mathematical truths would still hold even if no mathematicians existed.
Contrast: What Moral Objectivism Is Not

The best way to sharpen your understanding is to see what moral objectivism is opposed to:

Moral Subjectivism

This view says moral claims are just expressions of personal feelings or attitudes. "Murder is wrong" really just means "I don't like murder" — it's no different from saying "Ugh, murder!" There are no objective moral facts; there are only personal reactions. Moral objectivism directly denies this.

Moral Relativism

This view says moral truths are relative — they're true only relative to a culture, society, or historical period. So slavery might be "right" for ancient Rome and "wrong" for modern society, and neither culture is mistaken — they just have different moral frameworks. Moral objectivism directly denies this too. It says: one of those societies was wrong, even if it didn't know it.

Moral Nihilism

This view says there are no moral facts at all — morality is a kind of fiction or illusion. Moral objectivism is the opposite: it insists moral facts are real.

Moral Constructivism (a subtle one)

This view says moral facts are real, but they are constructed by rational agents — built through agreement, reason, or social contracts. Moral objectivism typically insists that moral facts are discovered, not constructed — they were already there, waiting to be found, like scientific facts about the physical world.
Why Would Anyone Believe Moral Objectivism?

Here are the strongest reasons philosophers have given:

1. The Moral Progress Argument

History shows what looks like genuine moral progress. We abolished slavery. We recognized women's rights. We banned torture. But the concept of "progress" only makes sense if there's an objective standard you're getting closer to. If morality were purely subjective or cultural, you couldn't say we "improved" — you could only say we "changed." Moral objectivism explains why calling the end of slavery moral progress makes sense: we moved closer to the truth.

2. The Strong Intuition Argument

Some moral convictions feel so rock-solid that denying them seems absurd. Almost no one, in any culture or era, genuinely believes that torturing babies for personal entertainment is a neutral or acceptable act. This near-universal, powerful intuition suggests we might be tracking a real moral fact, not just a cultural preference.

3. The Disagreement Doesn't Disprove Facts

People disagree about science and history all the time, and we don't conclude that there are no scientific or historical facts. Why should moral disagreement be different? Disagreement might just mean some people are wrong — not that there's no fact of the matter.

4. Moral Language Implies It

When people argue about morality, they behave as if they're debating facts. They give reasons, evaluate evidence, change their minds, and accuse others of being wrong — not just different. This common behavior suggests that ordinary moral discourse already presupposes moral objectivism.
The Main Versions of Moral Objectivism

Moral objectivism is a broad position, and philosophers have defended it in several distinct ways:

Moral Realism

The most straightforward form. It says moral facts are real features of the world, fully independent of minds, just like physical facts. Philosophers like G.E. Moore argued that "goodness" is a real, non-natural property that some things have — it can't be reduced to any physical or psychological description, but it's still objectively real.

Natural Law Theory

Associated with Aristotle and later Thomas Aquinas, this view grounds moral facts in human nature and reason. What is "naturally good" for a human being — what allows us to flourish as the kind of creatures we are — is objectively good. Moral truths aren't arbitrary; they flow from what human beings fundamentally are.

Rationalist Ethics (Kant)

Immanuel Kant argued that moral truths are grounded purely in reason. His famous "Categorical Imperative" says: act only according to rules you could consistently will to become universal laws. This is purely rational, objective, and applies to all rational beings everywhere — no culture or preference involved.

Divine Command Theory

Some religious thinkers hold that moral facts exist because God commands them. While controversial (see the "Euthyphro dilemma" below), this is a form of objectivism in that the moral truths exist outside of human opinion — they come from God's nature or will.

Moral Intuitionism

Philosophers like W.D. Ross held that certain moral truths — like "it's wrong to break a promise" or "it's good to help those in pain" — are self-evident to careful moral reflection, the way logical axioms are self-evident. We don't derive them from something else; we just see them clearly.
The Strongest Objections to Moral Objectivism

Being fair means taking the counterarguments seriously.

1. The Argument from Disagreement

If moral facts were objective, why do cultures disagree so dramatically about morality — on things like capital punishment, the ethics of war, animal rights, and more? Disagreement suggests there are no facts driving us toward a single truth. Objectivists respond: disagreement exists in science too, but we don't deny scientific facts. Disagreement might just mean some people are wrong.

2. Mackie's "Argument from Queerness"

Philosopher J.L. Mackie argued that if objective moral facts existed, they would be very strange things — unlike anything else in the universe. Physical facts can be detected by our senses. But how would you detect "wrongness" as a feature of the world? With what sense organ? And how would knowing a moral fact automatically motivate you to act on it? These are deeply puzzling questions without easy answers.

3. The Evolutionary Debunking Argument

Our moral intuitions likely evolved because they helped our ancestors survive and reproduce — not because they tracked moral truths. If evolution can fully explain why we have the moral feelings we do without positing any objective moral facts, then maybe those facts don't exist. Objectivists respond that evolution could have given us cognitive capacities that happen to track moral truths, just as it gave us cognitive capacities that track logical and mathematical truths.

4. The Euthyphro Dilemma (for Divine Command Theory)

Plato posed this sharp problem: Is something morally good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is already good? If the first, morality seems arbitrary (God could have commanded cruelty and made cruelty good). If the second, morality is independent of God — suggesting an objective moral order that exists above even God's will.
Common Misconceptions to Watch Out For

"Moral objectivism means everyone will agree." — No. Objective facts exist even when people disagree. The existence of objective moral truths doesn't guarantee that everyone will recognize them.

"Moral objectivism means we always know what's right." — No. Moral epistemology (how we know moral truths) is a separate question from moral metaphysics (whether they exist). Objectivists can readily admit that moral knowledge is hard to come by.

"Moral objectivism is arrogant or intolerant." — Not necessarily. Acknowledging that some things are objectively wrong (like genocide) doesn't mean you're intolerant of all differences. In fact, many objectivists argue we need objective moral facts to make sense of condemning real historical atrocities.

"Moral objectivism is the same as moral absolutism." — Not quite. Moral absolutism says moral rules have no exceptions (e.g., "lying is always wrong, no matter what"). Moral objectivism just says some moral truths are objective — it's compatible with the view that moral rules are nuanced and context-sensitive.
A Summary of the Whole Picture

Moral objectivism is a statement about the nature of morality. It says morality isn't just a human invention, a cultural convention, or an emotional reaction — it has real, mind-independent truth to it. Just as there are facts about physics and mathematics that no one invented, there are facts about right and wrong that we discover rather than create.

It stands against moral subjectivism (morality as personal feeling), moral relativism (morality as cultural agreement), and moral nihilism (morality as illusion). It is supported by the reality of moral progress, the power of shared moral intuitions, and the structure of moral language itself. It is challenged by the persistence of moral disagreement, the metaphysical strangeness of moral facts, and evolutionary explanations of moral feeling.

The debate is far from settled — it sits at the very center of metaethics, the branch of philosophy that studies the foundations and nature of morality itself. But understanding moral objectivism is the essential first step to understanding that entire debate.
